# Energy demand {#sec-demand}

This chapter explains how the model projects the use of each fuel in each sector of the economy, year by year. Fuel
use is the quantity at the heart of the model: emissions, revenues, the GDP effect and the household effects are all
fuel use multiplied by something else.

The core is one behavioural equation, the same for every sector and fuel: last year's use grows with GDP, shrinks with
autonomous efficiency gains, and responds to the after-tax price through two margins, how much the equipment is used
and how efficient it is. A handful of special cases sit around it: biofuels blended into road fuels, renewables used
outside the power sector, a possible shift of households from modern cooking fuels to biomass, and cooking fuel that is
initially exempt from price increases.

The chapter also computes electricity demand by sector, which it hands to the power model (@sec-power), and it closes
with the energy totals by sector group and fuel and their change against the baseline.

The methodology describes this block in
[methodology, section 3.3](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#sec-FuelConsumption). The prices that
drive it are built in @sec-prices; road fuel use under the engineer model is in @sec-transport; the GDP growth that
feeds the income term comes from @sec-fiscal.

**Indices.** Every equation holds for each scenario $o$ and country $c$, which are omitted. Sector (subsector) $s$,
fuel $f$, sector group $g$ and year $t$ are shown where they matter; electricity demand uses the demand group $d$. A
value of the baseline (scenario 1) in the same year carries the superscript $B$.

: Fuels and their keys {#tbl-dm-fuels}

Two more "fuels" appear outside this grid: renewables used directly in aviation and navigation
(@sec-dm-biofuels), and electricity, whose demand by sector is computed here but which is supplied by the power
model (@sec-dm-electricity).

Within one year the block runs in a fixed order. GDP growth is known first, because the GDP effect of a policy enters
one year later; electricity demand reads last year's power price; fuel use reads this year's after-tax prices, which
were computed for all years before the year loop.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A["GDP growth g(t)<br/>after the feedback"] --> B["Electricity demand<br/>by sector"]
  A --> C["Fuel use<br/>elasticity model"]
  P["After-tax and<br/>shadow prices"] --> C
  C --> D["Biofuels, renewables,<br/>leakage, exempt use"]
  D --> E["Fuel use<br/>used (ener)"]
  B --> W["Power model"]
  W --> T["Totals and change<br/>against the baseline"]
  E --> T
```

## The fuel-use equation {#sec-dm-fueluse}

Each year, fuel use in a sector is last year's use multiplied by five growth factors. This is the constant-elasticity
form of the methodology
([methodology, section 3.3.3](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#sec-FuelConsumptionDynamics)),
with three additions: the shadow price of non-pricing policies acts on the efficiency margin only, an additional
policy-induced efficiency gain joins the autonomous one, and the income elasticity is adjusted to the country's income
level.

In full ([M3.1](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M3-1)):

$$
\frac{F^{e}_{s,f,t}}{F^{e}_{s,f,t-1}} =
\left(\frac{1}{1 + \alpha_{s,f} + \alpha^{+}_{g(s)}}\right)^{1 + \epsilon_{U}}
\;\Psi_t\;
\left(1 + g_t\right)^{\epsilon_{Y}\, inc_t}
\left(\frac{p_{s,f,t}}{p_{s,f,t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_{U}}
\left(\frac{p_{s,f,t} + sh_{s,f,t}}{p_{s,f,t-1} + sh_{s,f,t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_{F}(1 + \epsilon_{U})}
$$ {#eq-dm-fueluse}

where

- $F^{e}_{s,f,t}$ is fuel use by the elasticity model (ktoe; code `enel`); in the base year $t_0$ it is the
  base-year use of the energy data (@sec-dm-data);
- $\epsilon_Y$, $\epsilon_U$, $\epsilon_F$ are the income, usage and efficiency elasticities of the fuel in the sector
  (they depend on the country, the fuel and the sector; the indices are dropped);
- $\alpha_{s,f}$ is the autonomous energy efficiency improvement (share per year) and $\alpha^{+}_{g(s)}$ the
  additional policy-induced efficiency gain of the sector's efficiency group (@sec-dm-aeei);
- $\Psi_t$ is the exogenous demand shock factor (@sec-dm-shock);
- $g_t$ is real GDP growth after the GDP feedback and $inc_t$ the income-level factor on the GDP elasticities
  (@sec-dm-income);
- $p_{s,f,t}$ is the after-tax price of the fuel in the sector (USD per GJ, real; code `atp`) and $sh_{s,f,t}$ the
  shadow price of non-pricing policies (USD per GJ; code `shp`), both from @sec-prices (@sec-dm-shadow).

The methodology writes the GDP term as $(Y_t / Y_{t-1})^{\epsilon_Y}$, total real GDP (not per capita). The model writes
the same ratio as $1 + g_t$.

The equation is easier to read as a product of named factors. Each is one idea:

$$
F^{e}_{s,f,t} = F^{e}_{s,f,t-1} \cdot A_{s,f} \cdot \Psi_t \cdot G_{s,f,t} \cdot U_{s,f,t} \cdot E_{s,f,t}
$$ {#eq-dm-factors}

| Factor | Formula | What it captures | Code |
|---|---|---|---|
| Efficiency factor $A$ | $\left(1 / (1 + \alpha + \alpha^{+})\right)^{1+\epsilon_U}$ | autonomous and additional efficiency gains, net of their rebound | `aef` |
| Shock $\Psi$ | $1 + \text{shock}_t \cdot \text{switch}$ | the legacy 2023-2024 calibration shock | `SHOCK` |
| Income term $G$ | $(1 + g_t)^{\epsilon_Y inc_t}$ | GDP growth, adjusted to the income level | `GDPI` holds $(1+g_t)^{inc_t} - 1$ |
| Usage term $U$ | $(p_t / p_{t-1})^{\epsilon_U}$ | how intensively existing equipment is used | |
| Efficiency term $E$ | $\left((p_t + sh_t)/(p_{t-1} + sh_{t-1})\right)^{\epsilon_F(1+\epsilon_U)}$ | how efficient the equipment is, net of rebound | `eff_exp` $= \epsilon_F(1+\epsilon_U)$ |

: The five growth factors of fuel use {#tbl-dm-factors}

The methodology assumes that all effects take place within the year: the elasticities are long-term elasticities
applied in one step. CPAT is therefore better suited to anticipated and progressively phased policies over the medium
term than to sudden shocks.

### Autonomous and additional efficiency {#sec-dm-aeei}

Equipment becomes more efficient over time even without new policies. The autonomous energy efficiency improvement
$\alpha$ captures this; the methodology sets it between 0.5% and 1% per year depending on the fuel and sector
([methodology, section 3.3.5.6](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#rates-of-technological-change-and-exogenous-rebound-effects)).

A scenario can add a policy-induced gain $\alpha^{+}$ for three groups of sectors:

$$
A_{s,f} = \left(\frac{1}{1 + \alpha_{s,f} + \alpha^{+}_{g(s)}}\right)^{1 + \epsilon_{U}}
$$ {#eq-dm-aef}

where

- $\alpha_{s,f}$ is the autonomous efficiency gain of the sector's elasticity sector and the fuel's autonomous
  efficiency fuel (@tbl-dm-sectors, @tbl-dm-fuels); gasoline and diesel take the oil value;
- $\alpha^{+}_{g(s)}$ is the scenario input of the sector's additional efficiency group (share per year, default 0).

| Additional efficiency group | Sectors | Scenario input (ScenarioDefinition row) |
|---|---|---|
| Road vehicles | road, rail, domestic aviation, domestic navigation | `AdditionalEfficiencyRoadVehicle` (243) |
| Residential | residential | `AdditionalEfficiencyResidential` (244) |
| Industrial | every other sector: food & forestry, services, the industry sectors, fuel transformation, other energy use | `AdditionalEfficiencyIndustrial` (245) |
| Power demand | electricity demand of every sector (@sec-dm-electricity) | `AdditionalEfficiencyPower` (242) |

: Additional policy-induced efficiency gains {#tbl-dm-addeff}

The exponent $1 + \epsilon_U$ (with $\epsilon_U < 0$) is the rebound: more efficient equipment makes each unit of
service cheaper, so part of the saving is used up by more use. The methodology puts this rebound from exogenous
efficiency between 20% and 60% across fuels and sectors.

### Income term, income-level adjustment and GDP feedback {#sec-dm-income}

Energy demand grows with the economy. The income term raises GDP growth to the power of the income elasticity, and the
income elasticity is scaled by a factor that depends on the country's GDP per capita:

$$
G_{s,f,t} = \left(1 + g_t\right)^{\epsilon_{Y}\, inc_t}
$$ {#eq-dm-income}

where $\epsilon_Y$ is the income (GDP) elasticity of the fuel in the sector, $g_t$ real GDP growth after the feedback,
and $inc_t$ the income-level factor.

**The income-level factor.** The literature finds that income elasticities rise as countries leave low income, peak
around lower-middle income (about USD 3,000 per capita) and then decline towards the level of developed countries
([methodology, section 3.3.5.2](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#income-elasticities)). The model
draws this reverse-U as a polynomial in log GDP per capita:

$$
x_t = \min\left(\bar{x},\ \ln y_{t-1}\right), \qquad
inc_t = \begin{cases}
\dfrac{\max\left(0,\ a x_t^4 + b x_t^3 + c x_t^2 + d x_t + e\right)}{n} & \text{if IncElAdj is Yes} \\[1ex]
1 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-dm-incfactor}

where

- $y_{t-1}$ is baseline real GDP per capita of the previous year (USD; in the base year, the base year's own value),
  from the macro series (real GDP over population);
- $\bar{x} = 10$ caps log GDP per capita (about USD 22,000, the methodology's "developed country" level);
- $a, \dots, e$ and $n$ are fixed constants (table below), $n = 0.74$ normalising the factor to the global average
  income elasticity of Burke and Csereklyei (2016);
- IncElAdj is the scenario switch "Adjust income elasticities for GDP levels?" (default `Yes*`; a starred Yes counts as
  Yes).

| Constant | Value | Role |
|---|---|---|
| $a$ (`IncfA`) | 0.012019 | coefficient of $x^4$ |
| $b$ (`IncfB`) | −0.365464 | coefficient of $x^3$ |
| $c$ (`IncfC`) | 4.011846 | coefficient of $x^2$ |
| $d$ (`IncfD`) | −18.722243 | coefficient of $x$ |
| $e$ (`IncfE`) | 31.75949 | constant (31.59949 + 0.16, as legacy) |
| $\bar{x}$ (`IncfLnCap`) | 10 | cap on log GDP per capita |
| $n$ (`IncfNorm`) | 0.74 | divisor |

: Constants of the income-level factor (sheet Constants; legacy Mitigation rows 2431-2433) {#tbl-dm-incf}

The factor is a data path: it is computed from baseline GDP per capita before the year loop (code `incp`, then
`inc.ela.adj` after the switch), so it is the same in every scenario. The same factor multiplies the GDP elasticities
of electricity demand (@sec-dm-electricity).

**The GDP feedback.** $g_t$ is not the baseline growth rate but growth after the effect of the policy's revenue use on
GDP ([methodology, section 4.7](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/04_Multipliers.html#sec-GDPFeedback)). The effect is
computed in @sec-fiscal and enters with a lag of one year, as a change in the GDP level:

$$
\ell_t = 1 + \epsilon^{GDP}_{t-1}, \qquad 1 + g_t = \left(1 + g^{0}_t\right)\frac{\ell_t}{\ell_{t-1}}
$$ {#eq-dm-gdpfeedback}

where $g^{0}_t$ is baseline real GDP growth (IMF WEO), $\epsilon^{GDP}_{t-1}$ last year's GDP effect (share of GDP;
0 when endogenous GDP effects are switched off) and $\ell_t$ the GDP level factor ($\ell_{t_0} = 1$; code `gdp.lvl`).
The baseline has no fiscal space of its own, so its growth is $g^{0}_t$. Because the effect is lagged, fuel use in
year $t$ never depends on revenue in year $t$: there is no circular reference. This is the "rebound" through GDP that
Appendix E of the methodology mentions under "Include endogenous GDP effects?".

**Residential biomass.** Residential biomass is treated as an inferior good by default: its income elasticity is set
to 0 unless the setting `BiomassNormal` ("Biomass is a normal good", read from the baseline column; default No) is Yes.

### Price terms: usage, efficiency and rebound {#sec-dm-price}

A higher price reduces fuel use through two margins
([methodology, section 3.3.5.3](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#price-elasticities)):

- the **usage** (intensive) margin: existing equipment is used less (fewer kilometres driven), elasticity $\epsilon_U$;
- the **efficiency** (extensive) margin: equipment is replaced by more efficient equipment, elasticity $\epsilon_F$.

$$
U_{s,f,t} = \left(\frac{p_{s,f,t}}{p_{s,f,t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_{U}}, \qquad
E_{s,f,t} = \left(\frac{p_{s,f,t} + sh_{s,f,t}}{p_{s,f,t-1} + sh_{s,f,t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_{F}(1 + \epsilon_{U})}
$$ {#eq-dm-priceterms}

where $p$ is the after-tax price and $sh$ the shadow price, both per GJ. The after-tax price
([M2.5](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M2-5)) includes existing taxes and subsidies, the new carbon tax, the auctioned ETS
cost, the new excise, the change in existing carbon pricing, the subsidy and price-control phase-outs, and VAT on all
of them; it has a floor of USD 0.01 per GJ. It is built in @sec-prices.

**Rebound.** When the shadow price is zero the two price terms combine into one:

$$
U_{s,f,t}\,E_{s,f,t} = \left(\frac{p_{s,f,t}}{p_{s,f,t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_{U} + \epsilon_{F} + \epsilon_{U}\epsilon_{F}}
$$ {#eq-dm-rebound}

The cross term $\epsilon_U \epsilon_F$ is positive (both elasticities are negative): it is the direct rebound, the
extra use of equipment that has become cheaper to run
([methodology, section 3.3.5.4](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#rebound-effect)). With
$\epsilon_U = \epsilon_F = -0.3$ the combined exponent is $-0.51$ instead of $-0.6$, so the rebound offsets about 15%
of the price response (the methodology quotes 15.5%, against 26-29% in a meta-analysis of 74 studies).

### Shadow prices of non-pricing policies {#sec-dm-shadow}

Some policies do not raise the fuel price but push towards more efficient equipment: feebates, efficiency regulations,
vehicle fuel-economy standards, and the free (output-based) allocation of an ETS. The model expresses each as a
**shadow price** per tonne of CO2, which enters the efficiency term only (@eq-dm-priceterms) and raises no revenue.
A regulation does not make fuel dearer to use, so it has no usage effect; it changes which equipment is bought.

Demand reads the shadow price per GJ ([M2.6](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M2-6)):

$$
sh_{s,f,t} = \Sigma_{s,t}\; ef_{s,f}
$$ {#eq-dm-shp}

where $ef_{s,f}$ is the calibrated CO2 emission factor (tCO2 per GJ; @sec-emissions) and $\Sigma_{s,t}$ the shadow
price of the sector (USD per tCO2; code `shpx`; [M1.4](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M1-4)), built in @sec-prices from
three parts:

$$
\Sigma_{s,t} = \underbrace{b_{g(s),t}\, a_{s}}_{\text{feebate}} \;+\; \underbrace{reg_{s,t}}_{\text{regulation}} \;+\; \underbrace{\tilde{p}^{E}_t\, \kappa_{s,t}\, \omega_{s,t}}_{\text{ETS free allocation}}
$$ {#eq-dm-shpx}

where

- $b_{g,t}$ is the feebate rate of the sector's feebate group (USD per tCO2) and
  $a_s = \mathbb{1}[\text{feebate covers } s] \times$ `SPPEffAdjFeebates` the share of the feebate on the efficiency
  margin (code `ssc`; ScenarioDefinition row 251, default 1);
- $reg_{s,t}$ is the regulation shadow price (below);
- $\tilde{p}^{E}_t$ is the tax-equivalent ETS price, $\kappa_{s,t}$ the new ETS coverage and $\omega_{s,t}$ the share
  allocated free (output-based) (@sec-emissions).

**Regulations as shadow prices.** The scenario's main policy (`ScenarioSelected`, ScenarioDefinition row 13) picks a
row of the legacy table of main scenarios. Explicit-pricing scenarios (carbon tax, total carbon price, coal excise, road
fuel tax, electricity emissions tax and excise) use the carbon price path as the carbon tax. Shadow-pricing scenarios
(feebates, power supply feebates, energy efficiency regulations, power feebate, vehicle fuel economy, residential and
industrial efficiency regulations, and "Baseline") have no explicit carbon tax; the carbon price path becomes a shadow
price:

$$
reg_{s,t} = \left(\tau_t - \tau^{x}_t\right) \cdot r \cdot \mathbb{1}[\text{the scenario covers } s]
$$ {#eq-dm-reg}

where $\tau_t$ is the carbon price path (code `cptraj`), $\tau^{x}_t$ the explicit carbon price (equal to $\tau_t$ in an
explicit scenario and 0 otherwise; code `cpx`), so the bracket is the shadow carbon price (code `cp.shd`); $r$ is the
efficiency adjustment of the scenario (code `regadj`) and the coverage comes from the scenario table (code `regc`).

| Efficiency adjustment | ScenarioDefinition row | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `SPPEffAdjEnergyEfficiencyRegulations` | 247 | 0.7 |
| `SPPEffAdjVehicleFuelEconomy` | 248 | 0.7 |
| `SPPEffAdjRes` (residential efficiency regulations) | 249 | 0.7 |
| `SPPEffAdjInd` (industrial efficiency regulations) | 250 | 0.7 |
| `SPPEffAdjFeebates` | 251 | 1 |

: Efficiency adjustments of shadow-pricing scenarios {#tbl-dm-regadj}

A text that is not in the scenario table counts as explicit pricing (the shipped scenarios use `" - Carbon tax"`). Power
demand responds to the same shadow prices through the costs of the power model (@sec-power). The shadow price is not removed for
exempt residential LPG and kerosene (@sec-dm-exempt), as legacy.

### Exogenous demand shock {#sec-dm-shock}

Legacy CPAT calibrates the first projection years to observed emissions with a one-off shock on energy demand. The
model keeps it as a factor:

$$
\Psi_t = 1 + \text{shock}_t \cdot \text{switch}
$$ {#eq-dm-shock}

where $\text{shock}_t$ is the country's shock (share; code `shock`) and the switch is the setting "Fuel use and power
demand: apply the legacy 2023-2024 shock" (Settings C19; 1 = on, the default, as legacy).

The shock values are typed calibration values of the legacy GHGs tab (rows 1202-1388, columns G and H), by country, for
the first two projection years (2023 and 2024) and 0 afterwards; a country without a value gets 0. For Egypt they are
−20.8% in 2023 and +9.2% in 2024. The same shock multiplies electricity demand, scaled there by
`EngineerModelProportionOfCovidFactor` (@sec-dm-electricity).

The methodology describes the shock as a Covid adjustment of 2020 and 2021, calibrated to emissions outturns
([methodology, section 3.3.4.4](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#sec-CalibrationCovid)). The model's
base year is 2022, so the shock that remains is legacy's 2023-2024 calibration.

### Elasticities and base-year fuel use {#sec-dm-data}

Every fuel and sector pair reads its parameters from one table, the fuel | subsector table (Excel-AI sheet Inputs
rows 5-148; [A3.2](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A3-2)).

**Elasticities** ([A3.1](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A3-1)). Legacy CPAT holds income, usage and efficiency elasticities for
8 elasticity fuels (coal, natural gas, gasoline, diesel, oil products, biomass, renewables, electricity) in 4 elasticity
sectors (transport, residential, industry, services), and autonomous efficiency gains for 6 fuels (coal, gas, oil,
biomass, renewables, electricity) in the same sectors. The country's value is read from the legacy Elasticities table
(column "Elasticity use"; Excel-AI sheet Inputs_ela). A fuel and sector pair takes the values of its elasticity fuel
and elasticity sector (@tbl-dm-sectors, @tbl-dm-fuels). A blank cell reads as 0.

The methodology explains how these values were chosen
([methodology, section 3.3.5](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#income-and-price-elasticities-of-demand)):
32 base income elasticities from Burke and Csereklyei (2016), adjusted for income levels after Gertler and others
(2016); price elasticities from the meta-study of Labandeira and others (2017), split into the usage and efficiency
margins and raised slightly for developing countries; all checked against in-house databases and other models.

**Base-year fuel use.** $F^{e}_{s,f,t_0}$ comes from one of two sources, chosen by `BalancesOrConsumption`
(ScenarioDefinition row 234; default Balances):

- **Balances:** the IEA energy balance flow of the sector, plus a second signed flow where there is one. Fuel
  transformation is the negative of own use plus heat (both flows with sign −1), so the residual between primary and
  final consumption becomes an additional industrial sector
  ([methodology, section 3.3.4.5](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#fuel-transformation)).
- **EnergyCons:** the CPAT energy consumption table (`enc.<fuel>` of the sector; blank or missing is 0).

**Other energy use** contains principally military fuel use; it follows the same equation
([methodology, section 3.3.4.6](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#other-energy-use)). Whether it is
taxed is a matter of coverage (@sec-prices).

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: fuel use by the elasticity model"}
```
# before the year loop (prices are known for every year)
for s in sectors:
    for f in fuels:
        alpha_add = AdditionalEfficiency[eff_group[s]]              # road vehicles / residential / industrial
        aef[s,f]     = (1 / (1 + alpha[s,f] + alpha_add)) ** (1 + eu[s,f])
        eff_exp[s,f] = ef[s,f] * (1 + eu[s,f])

# year loop
for t in years:
    g     = gdp.pos.pct[t]                                         # growth after the GDP feedback (lag 1)
    GDPI  = (1 + g) ** inc.ela.adj[t] - 1                          # income-level factor on the GDP elasticity
    SHOCK = 1 + shock[t] * ApplyDemandShock
    for s in sectors:
        for f in fuels:
            if t == t0:
                enel[s,f,t] = ener0[s,f]                           # energy balance or EnergyCons
            else:
                enel[s,f,t] = (enel[s,f,t-1] * aef[s,f]
                               * (1 + GDPI) ** ey[s,f]             # ey = 0 for residential biomass unless BiomassNormal
                               * (atp[s,f,t] / atp[s,f,t-1]) ** eu[s,f]
                               * ((atp[s,f,t] + shp[s,f,t]) / (atp[s,f,t-1] + shp[s,f,t-1])) ** eff_exp[s,f]
                               * SHOCK)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet Mitigation, sections 5-8, one block per sector with one row per fuel: rows `aef` (efficiency
  factor), `enel` (fuel use, elasticity model), `ener` (fuel use). The GDP growth raised to the income factor and the
  shock factor are helper rows of the section-0 header. Parameters: sheet Inputs rows 5-148 (the fuel | subsector
  table: elasticities, AEEI, additional efficiency group, efficiency exponent, base-year use), sheet Inputs_ela
  (elasticities of the country). Rows `incp`, `inc.ela.adj`, `shock` in section 3 (from the power paths, sheet
  Inputs_ppath). Inputs on ScenarioDefinition: `AdditionalEfficiencyRoadVehicle`, `AdditionalEfficiencyResidential`,
  `AdditionalEfficiencyIndustrial` (rows 243-245), `IncElAdj` (262), `GDPEndogenous` (267), `BalancesOrConsumption`
  (234), `ElPrcMainSrc`, `ElIncMainSrc` (223-224), `BiomassNormal` (326, baseline column); Settings C19 (shock switch).
- **CPAT Python:** `cpat_model/mitigation/fuel_use.py`: `prepare()` computes `aef` (with the price rows `atp`, `shp`),
  `step()` computes `enel`; `fuel_data.fuel_table()` builds the fuel | subsector table and
  `elasticity_data.elasticities()` reads the elasticities; `gdp.start()` computes `GDPI` and `SHOCK`;
  `power_data.power_paths()` the income factor path `incp`, and `power.prepare()` applies the switch
  (`inc.ela.adj`). Equations M3.1, A3.1, A3.2. Manual elasticities (`ElIncMainSrc` or `ElPrcMainSrc` = Manual) are not
  in CPAT Python yet; the run stops with a message.
- Order of calculation: [the blocks of CPAT Python](../CPAT_coded_documentation_html/02_How_it_works.html#sec-blocks)
  (`gdp.start`, `power.step`, `fuel_use.step`, `totals.energy`).
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT"}
- **LD21 (same as legacy, kept on purpose):** the fuel-use equation is CPAT equation 3.3.3 times the shock factor
  (switch Settings C19 on, as legacy; issue I92). GDP growth enters with the income factor (was issue I23). The
  additional policy efficiency gains are by scenario, as legacy, in three groups (road vehicles; residential;
  industrial = every other sector).
- **L66 (legacy bug, replicated):** other energy use belongs to the industrial group, so it takes the additional
  industrial efficiency gain; legacy applies no additional policy efficiency gain to its fossil fuels.
- **I24:** residential biomass has an income elasticity of 0 unless `BiomassNormal` = Yes (legacy row 5567).
- **LD1:** food & forestry uses the industry elasticities, the same as legacy (earlier prototype versions used the
  services elasticities).
- **Shadow prices (LD9; legacy bugs L87, L88 fixed):** in legacy the regulation share is 0 and the scenario's efficiency
  adjustments are read but never used, so regulations never act, and never reach power. The model applies them as in
  @eq-dm-reg, including power. The feebate share on the efficiency margin is `SPPEffAdjFeebates` (was the constant 1).
- **M13 (prototype bug, fixed):** the road vehicle feebate of the engineer road model adds the road regulation shadow
  price, not the carbon price, which is already in the fuel price.
- **Methodology:** the methodology's equation has one price ratio for both margins; the model puts the shadow price in
  the efficiency margin only, which the methodology also describes in words.
:::

## Biofuels, jet fuel and self-generated renewables {#sec-dm-biofuels}

A few fuels do not fit the grid of 9 fuels by 16 sectors
([methodology, section 3.3.4.1](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#biofuels-and-jet-fuel)). Jet fuel
is a fuel of its own, used in domestic aviation; it follows the fuel-use equation with the oil-products elasticities
and is priced at the kerosene price. Road biomass is split into three biofuels, and aviation and navigation can use
renewables directly ([A3.3](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A3-3)).

**Blended biofuels.** Bioethanol and biodiesel are blended into gasoline and diesel, so they follow the road use of the
fossil fuel they are blended into:

$$
B^{bgs}_t = B^{bgs}_{t-1}\,\frac{F^{e}_{rod,gso,t}}{F^{e}_{rod,gso,t-1}}, \qquad
B^{bdi}_t = B^{bdi}_{t-1}\,\frac{F^{e}_{rod,die,t}}{F^{e}_{rod,die,t-1}}
$$ {#eq-dm-blend}

where $B^{bgs}$ and $B^{bdi}$ are road bioethanol and biodiesel (ktoe; code `trbe`). Where last year's fossil use is 0
the biofuel holds its value.

**Other biofuels** follow the fuel-use equation with the oil | transport elasticities and autonomous efficiency, the
road vehicles additional efficiency, and the road biomass price:

$$
B^{obf}_t = B^{obf}_{t-1}\,
\left(\frac{1}{1 + \alpha^{oil,tra} + \alpha^{+}_{rod}}\right)^{1 + \epsilon_{U}}
\Psi_t \left(1 + g_t\right)^{\epsilon_{Y}\,inc_t}
\left(\frac{p_{rod,bio,t}}{p_{rod,bio,t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_{U}}
\left(\frac{p_{rod,bio,t} + sh_{rod,bio,t}}{p_{rod,bio,t-1} + sh_{rod,bio,t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_{F}(1+\epsilon_{U})}
$$ {#eq-dm-obf}

with $\epsilon_Y, \epsilon_U, \epsilon_F$ of oil products in transport (code `trp.bfe`; efficiency factor code
`trbea`). Road biomass is the sum of the three:

$$
F^{e}_{rod,bio,t} = B^{bgs}_t + B^{bdi}_t + B^{obf}_t
$$ {#eq-dm-roadbio}

The base-year biofuels are the road flows of the energy balance (bioethanol, biodiesel, other biofuels) or the
EnergyCons values, following `BalancesOrConsumption`.

**Self-generated renewables.** Renewable energy used directly in domestic aviation and navigation (base year: the
EnergyCons value `enc.ren` of the sector) follows the fuel-use equation with the renewables | transport elasticities,
the road vehicles additional efficiency and, as its price, the levelised investment cost of solar power from
@sec-power ([methodology, section 3.3.4.2](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#self-generated-renewables)):

$$
R_{s,t} = R_{s,t-1}
\left(\frac{1}{1 + \alpha^{ren,tra} + \alpha^{+}_{rod}}\right)^{1 + \epsilon_{U}}
\Psi_t \left(1 + g_t\right)^{\epsilon_{Y}\,inc_t}
\left(\frac{tic^{sol}_t}{tic^{sol}_{t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_{U} + \epsilon_{F}(1+\epsilon_{U})},
\qquad s \in \{avi, nav\}
$$ {#eq-dm-ren}

where $R_{s,t}$ is renewable use (ktoe; code `ener` with fuel `ren`), $tic^{sol}_t$ the levelised investment cost of
solar (USD per kWh; code `trpren`) and the elasticities those of renewables in transport (code `trp.rne`; efficiency
factor code `trrena`). There is no shadow price on this price. Renewables count in the sector, group and grand totals,
but not in any fuel total (@sec-dm-totals).

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: biofuels and self-generated renewables"}
```
for t in years:
    for b, fossil in (("bgs", "gso"), ("bdi", "die")):
        if t == t0:   trbe[rod,b,t] = road_biofuel_base[b]            # balance or EnergyCons
        elif enel[rod,fossil,t-1] == 0:   trbe[rod,b,t] = trbe[rod,b,t-1]
        else:         trbe[rod,b,t] = trbe[rod,b,t-1] * enel[rod,fossil,t] / enel[rod,fossil,t-1]
    trbea = (1 / (1 + aei[oil,tra] + AdditionalEfficiencyRoadVehicle)) ** (1 + usg[oil,tra])
    if t == t0:   trbe[rod,obf,t] = road_biofuel_base["obf"]
    else:
        trbe[rod,obf,t] = (trbe[rod,obf,t-1] * trbea * (1 + GDPI) ** inc[oil,tra]
                           * (atp[rod,bio,t] / atp[rod,bio,t-1]) ** usg[oil,tra]
                           * ((atp[rod,bio,t] + shp[rod,bio,t]) / (atp[rod,bio,t-1] + shp[rod,bio,t-1]))
                             ** (eff[oil,tra] * (1 + usg[oil,tra]))
                           * SHOCK)
    trbe[rod,bio,t] = trbe[rod,bgs,t] + trbe[rod,bdi,t] + trbe[rod,obf,t]

    trpren[t] = tic[pow,sol,t]
    trrena = (1 / (1 + aei[ren,tra] + AdditionalEfficiencyRoadVehicle)) ** (1 + usg[ren,tra])
    for s in ("avi", "nav"):
        if t == t0:   ener[s,ren,t] = enc_ren[s]
        else:
            r = trpren[t] / trpren[t-1]
            ener[s,ren,t] = (ener[s,ren,t-1] * trrena * (1 + GDPI) ** inc[ren,tra]
                             * r ** usg[ren,tra] * r ** (eff[ren,tra] * (1 + usg[ren,tra])) * SHOCK)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet Mitigation, section 5b (rows `trp.eb2` base-year road biofuels, `trbe`, `trbea`, `trp.bfe`,
  `trpren`, `trrena`, `trp.rne`, `trp.rn0`), and the rows `ener` of renewables in the aviation and navigation blocks
  (section 5).
- **CPAT Python:** `cpat_model/mitigation/fuel_use.py`, `step()` (block "biofuels in road transport, aviation and
  navigation"), with `_road_biofuel()` and `_renewable_use()` for the base year. Equation A3.3.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT"}
- **I143, I144:** the elasticities of other road biofuels (oil | transport) and of self-generated renewables
  (renewables | transport) are read as legacy rows 5392, 5406 and 5491, 5516 do.
- **Methodology:** the methodology places self-generated renewables in the buildings and industry sectors; the model,
  like legacy, has them only in domestic aviation and navigation, where the EnergyCons data hold them.
- Under the engineer road model (`TrModel` = Engineer) road biofuels come from @sec-transport instead.
:::

## Residential leakage to biomass {#sec-dm-leakage}

When modern cooking fuels become dearer, some households may switch back to traditional biomass. This "leakage"
reduces the emission savings and worsens household air pollution
([methodology, section 3.3.4.3](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#biomass-substitution-in-the-residential-sector);
air pollution effects in
[methodology, section 6.6.5](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/06_Air_pollution.html#leakage-to-biomass)).

The option is off by default. It is switched on by `BiomassLeakage` ("Include leakage to biomass in residential sector",
ScenarioDefinition row 325, read from the baseline column; on when it starts with "Yes"). It applies only to the
country's most-used cooking fuel, and only if that fuel is natural gas, LPG or kerosene
([A3.4](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-A3-4)).

The calculation runs in five steps for each leaking fuel $m \in \{nga, lpg, ker\}$ in the residential sector, from the
first projection year (all flows are 0 in the base year).

**Step 1: the new policy in the price.** Only new policies cause leakage, not movements of the international price:

$$
W_{m,t} = N_{res,m,t}\left(1 + v_m\right)
$$ {#eq-dm-lkt}

where $N_{res,m,t}$ is the total new policy per GJ of the residential row (new carbon tax, ETS cost and new excise;
code `nce`) and $v_m$ its VAT rate. An exempt fuel (@sec-dm-exempt) has no new policy, so it does not leak.

**Step 2: the share that leaks.** A rise in the new policy relative to last year's price moves a share of the fuel to
biomass:

$$
\pi_{m,t} = \mathbb{1}[\text{on},\ m = m^{*}] \cdot
\min\left( \left(1 + \frac{W_{m,t} - W_{m,t-1}}{p_{res,m,t-1}}\right)^{\sigma \eta_{bio} / (\eta_m L)} - 1,\ 1 \right)
$$ {#eq-dm-lkp}

where

- $m^{*}$ is the country's most-used cooking fuel (WHO cooking data, overall sample; LPG if the country has no entry);
- $\sigma$ is the cross-price elasticity of biomass with respect to LPG (default 0.25; legacy Elasticities C131, legacy
  row 360);
- $\eta_m$, $\eta_{bio}$ are the cookstove efficiencies of the fuel and of biomass (table below);
- $L$ is the substitution lag (1 year, sheet Constants; it divides the exponent);
- $p_{res,m,t-1}$ is last year's after-tax price of the fuel.

**Step 3: the change in fossil use.** The share is read as a share of useful energy, so it is weighted by the stove
efficiency of the fuel:

$$
d_{m,t} = -\left(F_{res,m,t-1} - X_{m,t-1}\right)\eta_m\,\pi_{m,t}
$$ {#eq-dm-lkd}

where $F_{res,m,t-1}$ is last year's actual fuel use (which already includes earlier leakage) and $X_{m,t-1}$ the
initially exempt use (@sec-dm-exempt; 0 unless that option is on), which does not leak.

**Step 4: the biomass that replaces it.** Biomass supplies the same useful energy:

$$
b_{m,t} = -d_{m,t}\,\frac{\eta_m}{\eta_{bio}}, \qquad \text{so that}\quad \eta_m d_{m,t} + \eta_{bio} b_{m,t} = 0
$$ {#eq-dm-lkb}

**Step 5: cumulative changes.** The yearly changes add up to level shifts that are added to residential fuel use:

$$
Lk_{m,t} = Lk_{m,t-1} + d_{m,t} + \left(X^{a}_{m,t} - X^{a}_{m,t-1}\right), \qquad
Lk_{bio,t} = Lk_{bio,t-1} + \sum_{m} b_{m,t}
$$ {#eq-dm-lkc}

where $X^{a}$ is the adjustment for initially exempt use (@eq-dm-exempt-adj; 0 unless that option is on), and
$Lk_{t_0} = 0$. The net change $\sum_m Lk_m + Lk_{bio}$ is reported as a memo row (code `lks`).

| Parameter | Symbol | Default | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Natural gas cookstove efficiency | $\eta_{nga}$ | 0.58 | `NatGasEff` (ScenarioDefinition row 301, baseline column) |
| LPG cookstove efficiency | $\eta_{lpg}$ | 0.56 | `LPGEff` (row 298) |
| Kerosene cookstove efficiency | $\eta_{ker}$ | 0.45 | `KerEff` (row 299) |
| Biomass cookstove efficiency | $\eta_{bio}$ | 0.20 | `BioEff` (row 300) |
| Cross-price elasticity of biomass w.r.t. LPG | $\sigma$ | 0.25 | Elasticities table (global) |
| Substitution lag | $L$ | 1 year | sheet Constants (`ResSubstLag`) |
| Most-used cooking fuel | $m^{*}$ | country data | WHO cooking table |

: Parameters of residential leakage (efficiencies from Malla and Timilsina, 2014) {#tbl-dm-leak}

How the leakage behaves:

- A **fall** in the new policy moves fuel back from biomass ($\pi < 0$). The share is capped at 1.
- A policy that rises and then stays flat moves fuel only in the years it rises. The shift then stays as a level
  shift: $Lk$ is not grown with GDP.
- With natural gas and a 10% rise in its price from new policies, the exponent is
  $0.25 \times 0.20 / 0.58 \approx 0.086$, so $\pi \approx 0.8\%$; the fossil change is $\pi \eta_{nga} \approx 0.5\%$ of
  gas use, replaced by $0.5\% \times 0.58/0.20 \approx 1.4\%$ of gas use in biomass (in ktoe).
- Every product of residential fuel use follows the leakage: CO2, CH4, local pollutants, revenues, the weights of the
  average prices and the distribution module. $F^{e}$ stays the elasticity model.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: residential leakage to biomass"}
```
on = BiomassLeakage.startswith("Yes")
for t in years:
    for m in ("nga", "lpg", "ker"):
        lkt[m,t] = nce[res,m,t] * (1 + vat[res,m])            # new policy in the price, with VAT
        if t == t0:
            lkp[m,t] = 0;  lkd[m,t] = 0
        else:
            expo = sigma * BioEff / Eff[m] / ResSubstLag
            active = 1 if (on and m == CookFuel) else 0
            lkp[m,t] = active * min((1 + (lkt[m,t] - lkt[m,t-1]) / atp[res,m,t-1]) ** expo - 1, 1)
            lkd[m,t] = -(ener[res,m,t-1] - lkx[m,t-1]) * Eff[m] * lkp[m,t]
        lkb[m,t] = -lkd[m,t] * Eff[m] / BioEff
    for m in ("nga", "lpg", "ker"):
        lkc[m,t] = 0 if t == t0 else lkc[m,t-1] + lkd[m,t] + (lkxa[m,t] - lkxa[m,t-1])
    lkcb[t] = 0 if t == t0 else lkcb[t-1] + sum(lkb[m,t] for m in ("nga", "lpg", "ker"))
    lks[t]  = sum(lkc[m,t] for m in ("nga", "lpg", "ker")) + lkcb[t]
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet Mitigation, section 6b, rows `lkt`, `lkp`, `lkd`, `lkb`, `lkc`, `lkcb`, `lkz` (a row of zeros
  for the sectors and fuels that do not leak), `lks`. The leakage rows are added to `ener` through the leakage position
  of the fuel | subsector table (Inputs column BF). Settings C59-C89 hold the switch, the cooking fuel, the stove
  efficiencies and the substitution elasticity.
- **CPAT Python:** `cpat_model/mitigation/fuel_use.py`, `leakage_settings()` (switch, most-used cooking fuel,
  efficiencies, elasticity) and `step()` (block "residential leakage to biomass"). Equation A3.4.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT"}
- **L45 (legacy bug, fixed):** legacy's leakage is inconsistent; the model gives kerosene its own price and share and
  computes the change on actual use, including earlier leakage.
- **L90 (legacy bug, fixed):** legacy multiplies the biomass replacement by the biomass efficiency again, which breaks
  the balance of useful energy; the model keeps $\eta_m d + \eta_{bio} b = 0$.
- **L91 (legacy bug, fixed):** in legacy an exempt residential fuel still leaks; the model reads the row's own new
  policy, which is 0 for an exempt fuel.
- **I138:** initially exempt use does not leak (the change is computed on use net of the exempt part).
- **I137:** LPG is the cooking fuel when the WHO code of the country is missing.
- **Methodology:** the methodology's example says a 10% price change moves 0.9% of natural gas use to biomass; with
  the defaults the leaked share $\pi$ is about 0.8%, and the model applies it to useful energy.
:::

## Exempt residential cooking fuel {#sec-dm-exempt}

Two options protect households' cooking fuel from new policies. Both act through the price or the quantity of the
residential rows.

**Always exempt residential LPG and kerosene.** With `AlwaysExemptResLPGKer` (ScenarioDefinition row 268, by
scenario; default `No*`; a starred `Yes*` counts as Yes) the new carbon tax, the new ETS cost and the new excise of the
residential LPG and kerosene rows are 0 (exemption factor, code `exf`; @sec-prices). Their after-tax price then keeps
only existing taxes, the change in existing carbon pricing and the subsidy phase-outs, so their demand responds only
to those. The shadow price stays, and so does their place in ETS-covered emissions where the residential sector is in
an ETS. Exempt fuels do not leak to biomass. Exemptions are introduced in
[user guide, section 1.2.4](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/01_User_Guide.html#exemptions).

**Initially exempt demand of the most-used cooking fuel.** With `ExemptMostCook` = Yes (row 312), the use of the
most-used cooking fuel by the bottom deciles of households is initially shielded from the price response, which is
phased in later. The shielded share $\chi$ is the spending of the bottom `ExemptCookDeciles` deciles (row 313, default
4) on the fuel, over the economy-wide spending on it: household survey budget share times consumption per capita times
the weight of each decile (Settings C83, `ExemptCookShare`).

The exempt use starts as a share of base-year use and then grows with the elasticity model, but with the usage response
to the price removed until the phase-in:

$$
X_{m,t_0} = \chi\,F^{e}_{res,m,t_0}, \qquad
X_{m,t} = X_{m,t-1}\;\frac{F^{e}_{res,m,t}}{F^{e}_{res,m,t-1}}\;\left(\frac{p_{res,m,t}}{p_{res,m,t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_U(\phi_t - 1)}
$$ {#eq-dm-exempt}

where $m$ is the most-used cooking fuel ($\chi = 0$ for the other fuels), $\epsilon_U$ its residential usage
elasticity, and $\phi_t$ the phase-in of the usage response:

$$
\phi_t = \begin{cases}
\min\left(\max\left(\dfrac{t + 1 - T^{pha}}{N^{pha}},\ 0\right),\ 1\right) & \text{if ExemptPhaseout} \\[1ex]
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-dm-phasein}

with $T^{pha}$ = `YearPha` (row 50, default 2027), $N^{pha}$ = `ExemptPhaseoutPeriod` (row 51, default 5 years) and
`ExemptPhaseout` (row 49, default FALSE). Where last year's use or price is 0, the ratio is taken as 1.

$F^{e}$ already contains the usage term $(p_t/p_{t-1})^{\epsilon_U}$; the last factor multiplies it by
$(p_t/p_{t-1})^{-\epsilon_U(1-\phi_t)}$, which takes out the share $1 - \phi_t$ of it. Before the phase-in the exempt use
keeps only the income, efficiency and shock terms; once $\phi_t = 1$ it responds like the rest.

The difference with the share of the elasticity model is added to residential fuel use through the leakage rows
(@eq-dm-lkc):

$$
X^{a}_{m,t} = X_{m,t} - \chi\,F^{e}_{res,m,t}, \qquad X^{a}_{m,t_0} = 0
$$ {#eq-dm-exempt-adj}

So residential use of the cooking fuel is $(1-\chi)F^{e} + X$ plus the leakage, and the leakage is computed on the use
that is not exempt.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: initially exempt cooking fuel"}
```
for t in years:
    lkxp[t] = clip((t + 1 - YearPha) / ExemptPhaseoutPeriod, 0, 1) if ExemptPhaseout else 0
    for m in ("nga", "lpg", "ker"):
        share = ExemptCookShare if m == CookFuel else 0
        if t == t0:
            lkx[m,t] = share * enel[res,m,t];   lkxa[m,t] = 0
        else:
            lkxe = 1 if enel[res,m,t-1] == 0 else enel[res,m,t] / enel[res,m,t-1]
            lkxr = 1 if atp[res,m,t-1] == 0 else atp[res,m,t] / atp[res,m,t-1]
            lkx[m,t]  = lkx[m,t-1] * lkxe * lkxr ** (eu[res,m] * (lkxp[t] - 1))
            lkxa[m,t] = lkx[m,t] - share * enel[res,m,t]      # enters lkc, so ener
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** exemption factor rows `exf` (section 1); sheet Mitigation, section 6b, rows `lkxp`, `lkxe`, `lkxr`,
  `lkx`, `lkxa`, entering `lkc`. Inputs on ScenarioDefinition: `AlwaysExemptResLPGKer` (268), `ExemptMostCook` (312),
  `ExemptCookDeciles` (313), `ExemptPhaseout`, `YearPha`, `ExemptPhaseoutPeriod` (49-51); Settings C83
  (`ExemptCookShare`, from the household survey).
- **CPAT Python:** `cpat_model/mitigation/fuel_use.py`: `prepare()` applies `exf`; `step()` computes `lkxp` to `lkxa`.
  The share needs the household survey deciles, which CPAT Python does not read yet: with `ExemptMostCook` = Yes the
  run stops with a message, and the share is 0 otherwise. Equation A3.4.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT"}
- **LD67 (same as legacy):** the initially exempt residential demand of the most-used cooking fuel is built as legacy
  rows 5568-5570; v0.9.0 (R6) takes the share over the economy-wide basket spend (I136), uses LPG if the WHO cooking
  code is missing (I137) and computes leakage on the use that is not exempt (I138).
- **L48 (legacy bug, fixed):** legacy's initially exempt rows have no income factor, and its exemption test misses a
  starred `Yes*`; the model grows the exempt use with the row's own elasticity path, income factor included.
- **L94 (legacy bug, fixed):** legacy's phase-in rules differ between rows; the model uses one rule (that of legacy rows
  2259-2265) everywhere.
- Always exempt LPG and kerosene: as legacy rows 5546-5547 (`IF(AlwaysExemptResLPGKer="Yes", 0, ...)`); the shadow
  price is not exempted, as legacy.
:::

## Fuel use used by the rest of the model {#sec-dm-ener}

The elasticity model $F^{e}$ is not always the fuel use that the rest of the model reads. Two things can replace or
adjust it: the road engineer model, and the residential adjustments above. The result is the fuel use $F$ (code
`ener`) used everywhere else ([M3.2](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M3-2)):

$$
F_{s,f,t} = \begin{cases}
F^{T}_{f,t} & s = \text{road},\ f \in \{gso, die, lpg, nga, bio\},\ \text{TrModel} = \text{Engineer} \\
F^{e}_{s,f,t} + Lk_{s,f,t} & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-dm-ener}

where

- $F^{T}_{f,t}$ is road fuel use from the engineer road model, calibrated to the energy balance in the base year
  (@sec-transport); it covers gasoline, diesel, LPG, natural gas and biofuels;
- $F^{e}$ is the elasticity model (@eq-dm-fueluse), with road biomass from @eq-dm-roadbio;
- $Lk_{s,f,t}$ is the cumulative residential leakage and exempt-use adjustment (@eq-dm-lkc) for residential natural
  gas, LPG, kerosene and biomass, and 0 for every other pair.

`TrModel` (ScenarioDefinition row 338) is Elasticity by default; then road fuel use stays the elasticity model's and
the engineer model's results go only to the transport co-benefits.

Everything downstream reads $F$: CO2 and other emissions (@sec-emissions), revenues and the GDP effect (@sec-fiscal),
the price averages and indices (@sec-prices) and the distribution module (@sec-distribution).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet Mitigation, sections 5-8, row `ener` of each fuel:
  `IF(engineer road row × tr.sw > 0, trkt, enel) + leakage row`; road biomass reads `trbe` instead of `enel`. The engineer
  road row and the leakage row are positions in the fuel | subsector table (Inputs columns AF and BF).
- **CPAT Python:** `cpat_model/mitigation/fuel_use.py`, `step()` (block "fuel use, emissions and revenues"). The
  engineer road model as the source of road fuel use is not in CPAT Python yet: with `TrModel` = Engineer the run stops
  with a message (`road.prepare`). Equation M3.2.
:::

## Electricity demand {#sec-dm-electricity}

Electricity demand by sector follows the same logic as fuel use, with its own elasticities by demand group. It is
computed at the start of the year, before the power model, which turns it into the generation required
(@sec-power). The methodology describes it in
[methodology, section 3.4.2.3](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#power-demand)
([M4.1](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M4-1)).

Sector policies (carbon tax, ETS, feebates, fuel price reform) act on electricity demand only through the electricity
price, which carries the policy cost of power generation. The demand price is a blend of last year's end-user prices,
so demand never depends on this year's power price:

$$
\bar{p}_{d,t} = w_d\,p^{res}_{t-1} + \left(1 - w_d\right) p^{ind}_{t-1}
$$ {#eq-dm-pdem}

where $p^{res}$ and $p^{ind}$ are the residential and industrial end-user electricity prices (USD per kWh, real;
@sec-power) and $w_d$ the weight of the residential price in demand group $d$. In the base year the demand price is the
price of the year before (data).

The demand multiple of each group combines the same terms as fuel use:

$$
M_{d,t} = \left(\frac{1}{1 + \alpha_d + \alpha^{+}_{pow}}\right)^{1 + \epsilon_{U,d}}
\left(1 + g_t\right)^{\epsilon_{Y,d}\,inc_t}
\left(\frac{\bar{p}_{d,t}}{\bar{p}_{d,t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_{U,d} + \epsilon_{F,d} + \epsilon_{U,d}\epsilon_{F,d}}
\left(1 + \text{shock}_t \cdot \text{switch} \cdot \kappa^{cov}\right)
$$ {#eq-dm-mult}

where

- $\alpha_d$, $\epsilon_{Y,d}$, $\epsilon_{U,d}$, $\epsilon_{F,d}$ are the electricity elasticities and autonomous
  efficiency gain of the group (electricity row of the elasticity table, in the group's elasticity sector);
- $\alpha^{+}_{pow}$ is `AdditionalEfficiencyPower` (ScenarioDefinition row 242, by scenario, default 0);
- $\kappa^{cov}$ is `EngineerModelProportionOfCovidFactor`, the share of the shock passed on to power demand
  (ScenarioDefinition row 372, default 1);
- there is no shadow price term: the shadow prices reach power through its own costs (@sec-power).

Demand of each sector is last year's demand times its group's multiple:

$$
E_{s,t} = \begin{cases}
E^{T}_{t} & s = \text{road and TrModel} = \text{Engineer} \\
E_{s,t-1}\,M_{d(s),t} & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\qquad E_{s,t_0} = \text{data}
$$ {#eq-dm-dem}

where $E_{s,t}$ is electricity demand (ktoe; code `dem`), $E^{T}$ road electricity from the engineer road model
(@sec-transport) and $d(s)$ the demand group of the sector (@tbl-dm-sectors). Demand covers 15 sectors (fuel
transformation has none). The base-year demand comes from the energy balance.

| Demand group $d$ | Sectors | Weight $w_d$ on the residential price | Elasticity sector |
|---|---|---|---|
| Transport | road, rail, aviation, navigation | 0.5 | transport |
| Residential | residential | 1 | residential |
| Industry | food & forestry, the industry sectors, other energy use | 0 | industry |
| Services | services | 0 | services |

: Electricity demand groups {#tbl-dm-elgroups}

The power model (@sec-power) adds up demand, $E_t = \sum_s E_{s,t}$, converts it into required generation and splits
consumption into residential and industrial users.

**A memo, not a fuel.** Electricity demand is shown in the sector blocks and summed by sector group (code `eldem`),
but it is not part of the fuel totals: the fuels burnt to generate it are (@sec-dm-totals). Nothing is counted twice.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: electricity demand"}
```
for t in years:
    for d in ("tra", "res", "ind", "srv"):
        pdem[d,t] = p2021[d] if t == t0 else w[d] * rp[res,t-1] + (1 - w[d]) * rp[ind,t-1]
        aeef = (1 / (1 + alpha[ecy,d] + AdditionalEfficiencyPower)) ** (1 + eu[ecy,d])
        mult[d,t] = 1 if t == t0 else (aeef
                     * (1 + gdp.pos.pct[t]) ** (ey[ecy,d] * inc.ela.adj[t])
                     * (pdem[d,t] / pdem[d,t-1]) ** (eu[ecy,d] + ef[ecy,d] + eu[ecy,d] * ef[ecy,d])
                     * (1 + shock[t] * ApplyDemandShock * EngineerModelProportionOfCovidFactor))
    for s in demand_sectors:                                   # 15 sectors, no fuel transformation
        if t == t0:                          dem[s,t] = dem0[s]
        elif s == "rod" and TrModel == "Engineer":  dem[s,t] = trkte[t]
        else:                                dem[s,t] = dem[s,t-1] * mult[group[s],t]
    demtot[t] = sum(dem[s,t] for s in demand_sectors)          # -> power: required generation
    for s in sectors: eldem[s,t] = dem[s,t] if s in demand_sectors else 0     # memo rows
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet Mitigation, section 3, part H: rows `pdem`, `aeef`, `mult`, `dem`, `demg`, `demtot`; memo rows
  `eldem` in the sector blocks and in section 11. Parameters: sheet Inputs rows 231-234 (demand groups: price weight,
  elasticities, base prices) and 238-252 (sectors: demand group, base-year demand, road flag).
- **CPAT Python:** `cpat_model/mitigation/power.py`, `step()` (block "demand"); memo rows `eldem` in
  `fuel_use.step()` and `totals.energy()`. Equation M4.1.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT"}
- **L1 (legacy bug, fixed):** in legacy, services electricity demand grows with the industrial multiple after 2023;
  here services keep the services multiple in every year.
- **L2 (legacy bug, fixed):** legacy's autonomous efficiency gain uses the efficiency elasticity in the exponent; here it
  uses the usage elasticity, as fuel use.
- **L3 (legacy bug, fixed):** legacy applies the income factor twice and anchors it to 2023; here it multiplies the GDP
  elasticity once.
- **LD24 (same as legacy):** the 2023-2024 demand shock applies to power demand too, switch Settings C19, on by default.
- **LD21:** power demand takes `AdditionalEfficiencyPower` of its own scenario, like every power input.
- **Methodology:** the methodology writes a GDP elasticity $\epsilon_G$ that it does not define; the model uses
  $\epsilon_Y$ with the income factor. The demand price is lagged one year on purpose (legacy rows 3687-3689).
:::

## Energy totals and changes against the baseline {#sec-dm-totals}

The last step adds fuel use up by sector group and by fuel, adds the fuels burnt in power plants, and compares every
total with the baseline of the same year ([M3.3](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M3-3)).

**By sector.** The total of a sector is the sum over its fuels, plus renewables in aviation and navigation:

$$
F_{s,t} = \sum_{f} F_{s,f,t} + R_{s,t}\,\mathbb{1}[s \in \{avi, nav\}], \qquad
F_{g,t} = \sum_{s \in g} F_{s,t}
$$ {#eq-dm-sectortotal}

for the sector groups $g$ transport, buildings, industry and other energy use (@tbl-dm-sectors).

**Power.** The power group is the fuel input of power generation, coal, gas, oil and biomass (code `pet`; @sec-power):

$$
F_{pow,t} = \sum_{k \in \{coa,\, nga,\, oop,\, bio\}} F^{pow}_{k,t}
$$ {#eq-dm-powtotal}

Nuclear, wind, solar, hydro and other renewables have no fuel input in this total.

**By fuel and in total.**

$$
F_{f,t} = \sum_{s} F_{s,f,t} + F^{pow}_{f,t}, \qquad
F_t = \sum_{s} F_{s,t} + F_{pow,t}
$$ {#eq-dm-fueltotal}

where $F^{pow}_{f,t}$ is the generation fuel use of the type that burns fuel $f$ (0 for the other fuels). Renewables
in aviation and navigation are in $F_t$ but in no fuel total. A check row confirms that the totals agree:

$$
\left|\sum_{s} F_{s,t} + F_{pow,t} - F_t\right| + \left|\sum_{f} F_{f,t} + R_{avi,t} + R_{nav,t} - F_t\right| = 0
$$ {#eq-dm-check}

**Change against the baseline.** Each total $x$ (the 9 fuel totals, the 4 sector groups, power and the grand total) is
compared with the baseline value of the same year:

$$
\Delta F_{x,t} = F_{x,t} - F^{B}_{x,t}, \qquad
\%\Delta F_{x,t} = \begin{cases} \dfrac{\Delta F_{x,t}}{F_{x,t} - \Delta F_{x,t}} & F_{x,t} - \Delta F_{x,t} \ne 0 \\[1ex] 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
$$ {#eq-dm-change}

where $F^{B}_{x,t}$ is scenario 1's value in the same year (codes `echg` and `epct`). In the baseline itself the
change is 0. The grand total also has its baseline value and percentage change as rows (`ener.ref`, `ener.pct`
$= F_t / F^{B}_t - 1$).

**Electricity totals.** Electricity demand (memo) is summed by sector group and in total:
$E_{g,t} = \sum_{s \in g} E_{s,t}$, $E_t = \sum_g E_{g,t}$ (code `eldem`).

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: totals and change against the baseline"}
```
for t in years:
    for s in sectors:
        ener[s,all,t] = sum(ener[s,f,t] for f in fuels) + (ener[s,ren,t] if s in ("avi", "nav") else 0)
    for g in ("tra", "bld", "ind", "oen"):
        ener[g,all,t] = sum(ener[s,all,t] for s in sectors if group[s] == g)
    ener[pow,all,t] = pet[t]                                     # coal, gas, oil, biomass burnt in power plants
    for f in fuels:
        ener[all,f,t] = sum(ener[s,f,t] for s in sectors) + (pe[pow,f,t] if f in power_types else 0)
    ener[all,all,t] = sum(ener[s,all,t] for s in sectors) + ener[pow,all,t]
    ener.chk[t] = (abs(sum(ener[s,all,t] for s in sectors) + ener[pow,all,t] - ener[all,all,t])
                   + abs(sum(ener[all,f,t] for f in fuels) + ener[avi,ren,t] + ener[nav,ren,t] - ener[all,all,t]))
    ener.ref[t] = baseline.ener[all,all,t];   ener.pct[t] = ener[all,all,t] / ener.ref[t] - 1
    for x in [(all,f) for f in fuels] + [(g,all) for g in ("tra","bld","ind","oen","pow")] + [(all,all)]:
        echg[x,t] = ener[x,t] - baseline.ener[x,t]
        epct[x,t] = 0 if ener[x,t] - echg[x,t] == 0 else echg[x,t] / (ener[x,t] - echg[x,t])
    for g in ("tra", "bld", "ind", "oen"):
        eldem[g,t] = sum(eldem[s,t] for s in sectors if group[s] == g)
    eldem[all,t] = sum(eldem[g,t] for g in ("tra", "bld", "ind", "oen"))
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet Mitigation, section 11 (rows `ener` by group, fuel and in total, `eldem`, `ener.chk`,
  `ener.ref`, `ener.pct`) and sub-block 11b (rows `echg`, `epct`). The baseline value is read through a helper row that
  finds scenario 1's column of the same year (REFCOL). Section 11 ends with two summary rows: total energy use and its
  change against scenario 1 (`echg.all`). The energy-balance matrix of legacy (block G) is not built as rows: it is a
  rearrangement of section 11.
- **CPAT Python:** `cpat_model/mitigation/totals.py`, `energy()`, with `reference()` for the baseline value; the sector
  and group totals of the four groups are set at the end of `fuel_use.step()`. Equation M3.3. In the results the code
  `ener.all.all` is written as Excel-AI's `ener.tot.tot`.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT"}
- **LD39 (same as legacy):** generation fuel use (coal, gas, oil, biomass) is in the fuel totals; electricity final
  demand is a memo.
- The change against the baseline replaces legacy's post-processing block F7.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check: results for Egypt"}
Values of Excel-AI 1.1.0 for Egypt (`coded/cpat_testing/compare/reference/excel_ai_1.1.0.csv`), which CPAT Python
reproduces (test "fuel use by subsector": pass). Scenario 1 is the baseline; scenario 2 a carbon tax of USD 20 per
tCO2 from 2027. Leakage to biomass and the exemptions are off.

**Baseline energy use (ktoe).**

| Group | 2022 | 2023 | 2030 | 2041 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Transport | 18,799 | 19,280 | 27,128 | 34,169 |
| Buildings | 7,283 | 7,815 | 10,023 | 11,412 |
| Industry | 21,715 | 20,178 | 28,784 | 40,075 |
| Other energy use | 96 | 83 | 117 | 165 |
| Power (fuel input) | 33,221 | 31,499 | 44,396 | 47,996 |
| **Total** | **81,114** | **78,856** | **110,448** | **133,816** |

- The 2023 shock (−20.8%) outweighs GDP growth (3.8%) and the fall in prices: total energy use falls 2.8% in 2023,
  then rises 17% in 2024 (shock +9.2%) to 92,610 ktoe.
- The income-level factor is 1.027 in 2022 and 2023, 0.970 in 2030 and 0.946 in 2041: Egypt's GDP per capita is past
  the peak of the reverse-U.
- Residential biomass declines from 1,495 ktoe (2022) to 1,210 (2041): its income elasticity is 0.
- Electricity demand of buildings rises from 10,743 ktoe (2022) to 16,868 (2030); industry from 3,606 to 4,924;
  transport from 43 to 66.

**Change against the baseline in 2030, carbon tax scenario.**

| Total | Change (ktoe) | Change (%) |
|---|---|---|
| Transport | −2,601 | −9.6 |
| Buildings | −1,861 | −18.6 |
| Industry | −4,601 | −16.0 |
| Other energy use | −0.1 | −0.06 |
| Power (fuel input) | −3,370 | −7.6 |
| Coal | −284 | −13.3 |
| Natural gas | −4,938 | −9.7 |
| Gasoline | −988 | −8.3 |
| Diesel | −2,865 | −12.9 |
| LPG | −1,120 | −16.2 |
| Other oil products | −2,149 | −14.9 |
| Biomass | 0 | 0 |
| **Total** | **−12,432** | **−11.3** |

Before 2027 the two scenarios differ by about 22 ktoe, all in power fuel use; sector
demand is identical. GDP growth after the feedback is 4.70% in 2030 against 4.84% in the baseline.

**Against legacy CPAT (Egypt baseline, 129 fuel-use rows).** In 2022 81% of the rows are within 1% of legacy and 91%
within 5%; from 2025 about 80% are within 1%. The largest gap in 2030 is fuel transformation diesel (legacy 883,
model 1,386 ktoe). The gaps follow the newer price data (prices from 2024 instead of 2022) and the fixed fuel-use bugs;
the base year uses the same energy balance.
:::

## Summary of variables {#sec-dm-variables}

| Symbol | Meaning | Unit | Code |
|---|---|---|---|
| $F^{e}_{s,f}$ | fuel use, elasticity model | ktoe | `enel` |
| $F_{s,f}$ | fuel use used by the rest of the model | ktoe | `ener` |
| $A_{s,f}$ | efficiency factor (autonomous and additional) | factor | `aef` |
| $\alpha_{s,f}$, $\alpha^{+}_{g}$ | autonomous and additional efficiency gains | share per year | `alpha`; `AdditionalEfficiency*` |
| $\epsilon_Y, \epsilon_U, \epsilon_F$ | income, usage and efficiency elasticities | | `ey`, `eu`, `ef` (Python); Inputs columns |
| $inc_t$ | income-level factor on the GDP elasticities | factor | `incp`, `inc.ela.adj` |
| $(1+g_t)^{inc_t} - 1$ | GDP growth raised to the income factor | share | `GDPI` |
| $g_t$, $\ell_t$ | GDP growth after the feedback, GDP level factor | share, factor | `gdp.pos.pct`, `gdp.lvl` |
| $\Psi_t$, $\text{shock}_t$ | demand shock factor, shock | factor, share | `SHOCK`, `shock` |
| $p_{s,f}$, $sh_{s,f}$ | after-tax price, shadow price | USD/GJ | `atp`, `shp` |
| $\Sigma_s$, $reg_s$, $a_s$ | shadow price by sector, regulation part, feebate share | USD/tCO2, share | `shpx`, `reg`, `ssc` |
| $\tau_t - \tau^{x}_t$, $r$ | shadow carbon price, efficiency adjustment | USD/tCO2, share | `cp.shd`, `regadj` |
| $B^{bgs}, B^{bdi}, B^{obf}$ | road biofuels | ktoe | `trbe` |
| $R_{s}$, $tic^{sol}$ | renewables in aviation and navigation, their price | ktoe, USD/kWh | `ener` (fuel `ren`), `trpren` |
| $W_m$, $\pi_m$, $d_m$, $b_m$ | leakage: new policy in the price, leaked share, fossil change, biomass | USD/GJ, share, ktoe | `lkt`, `lkp`, `lkd`, `lkb` |
| $Lk_m$, $Lk_{bio}$ | cumulative leakage added to fuel use | ktoe | `lkc`, `lkcb` (none: `lkz`; net: `lks`) |
| $\phi_t$, $X_m$, $X^{a}_m$ | exempt use: phase-in, exempt use, adjustment | share, ktoe | `lkxp`, `lkx`, `lkxa` (ratios `lkxe`, `lkxr`) |
| $\bar{p}_d$, $M_d$ | electricity demand price, demand multiple | USD/kWh, factor | `pdem`, `mult` (efficiency `aeef`) |
| $E_s$, $E$ | electricity demand by sector, total | ktoe | `dem`, `demtot`; memo `eldem` |
| $F_g$, $F_f$, $F$ | totals by group, by fuel, grand total | ktoe | `ener` (`all` rows) |
| $F_{pow}$ | fuel input of power generation | ktoe | `pet` |
| $\Delta F$, $\%\Delta F$ | change against the baseline | ktoe, % | `echg`, `epct`; `ener.ref`, `ener.pct` |

: Variables of the energy demand block {#tbl-dm-variables}
